@DamonZwicker
Damon — really appreciate how deeply you read the spec. Your four points were spot on and each one made the spec better. Where they landed:

1. The double-rounding one was the hardest to get right, and honestly it sent me back to the drawing board. Replacing median + MAD with trimmed mean, tail trimming handles outliers by construction, and because it's a multi-point mean there's no half-ULP ambiguity to fight with. Kept precision×2 internally with a single quantize at comparison so the rounding guarantee is still there even if someone implements a different algorithm.

2. Continuous gas — sorted input is the challenger's job. The contract just walks the array once and checks each value is ≤ the next, O(n). No on-chain sort means no griefing surface. The challenger has skin in the game — they want to win, so they'll sort. The contract doesn't need to trust them, it just rejects unsorted data.

3. Your point about params alone not pinning w was exactly right. If all you commit is params, someone swaps the classifier contract after the outcome is observable and nobody can tell. Commitment is now (scopeRoot, classifier, paramsHash) — scope root, classifier address, and params together. None can move after the fact. Tiago's Layer2PreCheck already binds them in the Market struct, so the reference impl already does this — the spec just needed to say it out loud.

4. Revert on preconditions — kept the error types in the implementer's hands, just made it normative that preconditions revert with an informative message. A classifier that silently accepts bad input is worse than one that reverts opaquely, and what "informative" means can vary between a simple string and a custom error — implementer's choice.

Scope contestation, normative additions (first cut)

RESOLVED MEANING (meaning axis)

A contest MUST be evaluated against the market's actual resolved readings, not against any coordinate-complete witness set the contester is free to choose. verifyValueFidelity MUST require that the contester's (sourceId, value) pairs reproduce the readings fixed by a resolution-time commitment that was committed before the outcome was observable. The admissible verdict is therefore S1, X was material to THE resolution, and only S1.

The weaker reading S2, X was material to some coordinate-complete a the contester chose, is NOT offered as an alternative robustness mode. It is excluded by construction: material to some coordinate-complete a does not re-derive to a single answer from public data, so it cannot satisfy the recomputability MUST. Recomputability forces meaning to actual-resolution, it is not a configuration the spec toggles. Implementations MUST NOT expose an S2 / robustness-mode path. This retires the S1/S2 mode distinction for the meaning axis.

verifyValueFidelity is the value-half dual of the coordinate half: verifyAbsence and verifyScopeComplete bind which coordinates a may contain, verifyValueFidelity binds the values those coordinates MUST carry. Same bind-then-recompute shape, and contest() MUST enforce in order: verifyAbsence -> verifyScopeComplete -> verifyValueFidelity -> isolation -> classify.

PROVENANCE (type-1 / type-2) IS ORTHOGONAL TO THE MEANING AXIS

The split is provenance only. It does not change the verdict (S1) or the verifyValueFidelity interface, which MUST NOT fork.
•⁠  ⁠type-1 (chain-native): values recomputable from chain state at a pre-committed block pin, no separate commitment carried, verifyValueFidelity recomputes from chain and requires equality with a's value.
•⁠  ⁠type-2 (off-chain): chain cannot recompute, so a's (id, value) pairs are checked against a resolution-time commitment keccak256(abi.encode(sortedLeaves)) committed on-chain pre-outcome.

For type-2 the source-authenticated inputHash decomposes into two composed primitives, NOT one: (1) ERC-8281 observation commitment, commit the digest on-chain pre-outcome, and (2) zkTLS / input-provenance, authenticate the readings came from the claimed source. verifyValueFidelity covers (1), the commitment side, only. Source-authentication is the orthogonal zkTLS leg: it answers are these readings authentic, not does a match the committed readings. Both are required for the full S1 guarantee under off-chain provenance, and each MUST remain independently recomputable.

PRE-OUTCOME MUST (inherited): the resolution-time commitment MUST be committed before the outcome is observable. A post-outcome commitment does not satisfy this, it would only certify a value a committer fudged after seeing the result.

### Step 7 — Reputation (ERC-8275 reputation axis, from ERC-8299/WYRIWE attestations) — *babyblueviper1*

The reputation step establishes that an agent's standing is a value DERIVED from its public record of authentic verdicts resolved against settled outcomes. It establishes a derived measure, never an asserted score: a conformant Step 7 answers "is this value recomputable from the public attestation and outcome record," and MUST NOT be read as "a score a trusted party maintains." There is no scorer to trust; the record is the score.

A reputation step is conformant if and only if all of the following hold, each checkable from public data with no trust in any intermediary:

1. Derived, not stored. Reputation MUST be a deterministic function of public inputs, f(attestationCount, counterpartyDiversity, winRate, volumeCap), recomputable by any party from the attestation record and the settled outcomes. No mutable, updater-controlled score; no trusted scorer. The same inputs MUST produce the same value.

2. Signature-gated attestations. attestationCount MUST count only distinct verdict `event_id`s whose signature verifies against the validator's published key. Unsigned, forged, or self-asserted entries MUST NOT count, so reputation cannot be self-inflated.

3. Outcome-resolved, commit-gated, losses retained. winRate MUST be read from the public, non-editable settled outcomes, counting only outcomes whose settlement postdates the verdict's committed_at (the Step 4 anchor). Losses MUST remain in the record. A feed that surfaces only wins is non-conformant: it is marketing, not reputation.

4. Counterparty-weighted, not volume-gameable. counterpartyDiversity MUST count distinct at-stake counterparties, derived from inputHash, never call volume. The volume weight MUST be ceilinged by outcome-weight (`volumeCap`) so that call-spam or self-dealing cannot inflate the value.

5. Axis separation. Reputation MUST derive only from the per-action attestation axis (ERC-8299/WYRIWE). It MUST NOT read the per-period settler or compensation commitment. Infrastructure economics, meaning who relayed how many records and who was paid, MUST NOT leak into agent scoring.

6. Recomputable end-to-end. Any party holding the public attestation record MUST be able to recompute the value with no private state and no issuer assertion: verify each verdict signature against the published key; establish committed_at from the anchor (Step 4); follow each verdict's settled digests to win or loss on the public account, confirming each settlement postdates committed_at; then apply f(...) deterministically.

Layer 1 and 2 are the attack side: they falsify completeness by exhibiting omissions and proving materiality. But there's no defense side yet, and nobody has named it.

The gap: an honest agent who got it right has no way to accrue standing for getting it right. It can only avoid being nominated. The first question any real client asks — "which agent is actually good?" — the stack can only answer "the ones nobody happened to catch." That's the missing half.

Layer 3 is the defense side: a completeness bond. A party stakes a claim that a committed scope is sufficient under a pre-committed public w — a standing, funded invitation to falsify. It can never be proven; it can only survive. The longer it stands under an open bounty, the stronger the signal — exactly as an unclaimed bug bounty live for two years outweighs a fresh audit. Lindy completeness.

The core design decision that makes it coherent: the bond is slashable only by a Layer-2 materiality proof — a coordinate both absent from the committed scope (Layer 1) and material under the committed w (Layer 2). A bare Layer-1 nomination does NOT slash. This is the difference between a claim of exhaustiveness (impossible — E-capture guarantees something is always omitted, so every such bond dies) and a claim of sufficiency (achievable — no material omission under w). The bond claims F★-completeness: the minimal sufficient set from the paper, made into an economic primitive.

Was looking at how OpenAI and Anthropic manage their official SDKs — turns out they don't hand-write each language's SDK separately. They maintain one internal spec, and everything (Python, TS, Go, Java, Ruby...) is auto-generated from that single source. Anthropic actually uses a tool called Stainless to do this. So when the API changes, they update the spec, regenerate, done. All languages stay in sync automatically.

Got me thinking — could we do something similar for our ERC contracts?

The rough idea is a layered architecture like this:

Layer 0 — Spec (ABI / ERC interfaces)
This is the single source of truth. We own and maintain this. Solidity interfaces + compiled ABI JSON. Everything downstream is generated from here.

Layer 1 — Multi-language SDKs
Generated from the ABI automatically. Each SDK has two parts: a generated/ folder that's never manually edited, and a thin hand-written layer on top that provides a clean stable API. When spec changes, only the generated part regenerates — the hand-written layer stays stable. We'd support TS, Go, Python, Rust etc.

Layer 2 — MCP Server
This sits above the SDKs and exposes everything as MCP tools so AI agents can call our contracts directly. Primary path is calling through one of the SDKs. But here's the interesting part — if the SDK hasn't caught up with a new spec change yet, the MCP server can fall back to calling the contract directly using the raw ABI. So there's never a gap where something is in spec but not callable.

Layer 3 — Applications
Built by ecosystem developers on top of the SDKs or MCP. We don't own this layer.

For consistency across all of this, the idea is to have a shared vectors.json in the repo — basically golden test cases that every SDK and the MCP server all run against. So if TS and Go and the MCP fallback all agree on the same input/output, we know they're all correct and consistent.

All of this would live in one monorepo so a spec change and the regenerated SDKs land in the same PR, nothing gets out of sync.

One optimization point regarding input parameters: the current design passes full set A and full set B, then computes the difference B minus A on-chain. This brings two downsides:

1. Higher gas consumption — storing and iterating full A & B to calculate set difference costs substantial gas.

2. Complex isolation calculation logic — implementing set subtraction inside the contract is cumbersome and error-prone.

Proposed adjustment: instead of passing full B, we pass the base set A plus only the delta part (the extra coordinates from B \ A).
When running the isolation guard check, we no longer need to compute the difference on the fly; validation logic becomes much simpler and cleaner to implement. This parameter passing pattern is preferable for lower gas and simpler contract code.
